Let’s dive into Chapter 3: Focusing on Interests, Not Positions—Uncovering What Really Matters.
At the heart of every negotiation, there’s something deeper than just what people say they want.
Think about it—positions are the demands folks make, but underneath those demands are their real interests. Their needs, their worries, their hopes.
If everyone just digs in and argues over positions, things get stuck fast. But when you take the time to explore what’s really driving those positions, suddenly there’s room for new ideas and creative solutions.
Picture this: two siblings fighting over the last slice of cake.
One says, “I want it!” The other says, “No way, it’s mine!” If they keep arguing like that, they’re just going in circles.
But what if they pause and ask each other why the cake matters so much? Maybe one’s just hungry, and the other wants to save it for a friend.
Now, they can talk it out. Maybe they split the cake, or maybe they find another treat.
By focusing on the reasons behind the positions, they find a way forward.
Here’s the thing—interests are often hidden. People don’t always say them out loud, and sometimes, they don’t even realize what’s driving them.
So, how do you get to the heart of it?
It takes a bit of patience, a little curiosity, and some practical steps:
First, try asking “Why?” and “Why not?” when someone takes a position.
What are they hoping to gain? What are they trying to avoid?
These simple questions can reveal a lot more than you might expect.
Next, remember—each side usually has more than one interest.
Maybe there are practical needs, emotional reasons, or long-term goals all mixed together.
It’s rarely just about one thing.
Then, look for shared interests.
Chances are, both sides want something in common—like a fair process, a solution that lasts, or a good relationship moving forward.
And don’t forget to acknowledge differences.
Not everything will line up perfectly, and that’s totally normal.
Knowing where interests diverge just shows you what needs extra attention.
Let’s bring this idea to life with a real-world example:
Imagine a salary negotiation. An employee asks for more money, and the employer pushes back.
But if they talk openly about what really matters, maybe the employee admits they want recognition and a chance to grow, not just a bigger paycheck.
Meanwhile, the employer’s worried about budgets but wants to keep good people.
Understanding these interests, they might come up with options like bonuses, flexible hours, or training opportunities.
Shifting your focus from arguing over demands to exploring motivations is a game changer.
It’s like digging below the surface of a frozen lake—only then do you see the real currents shaping what’s above.
When everyone understands each other’s interests, it’s so much easier to find solutions that work for all sides.
